segments.text: Light travels along a silicon wire, a waveguide, and we want to split it evenly into two.
segments.say: Light travels along a silicon wire, a waveguide, and we want to split it evenly into two.

segments.text: A person would draw a smooth fork. Squeezed into this small box, it delivers only 86% of the light.
segments.say: A person would draw a smooth fork. Squeezed into this small box, it delivers only eighty-six percent of the light.

segments.text: A computer drew this instead: a strange, organic pattern in the same box. It delivers 99.8%.
segments.say: A computer drew this instead: a strange, organic pattern, in the same box. It delivers ninety-nine point eight percent.

segments.text: How does a computer invent shapes no human would draw?
segments.say: How does a computer invent shapes no human would draw?

segments.text: The trick is to run light backward. It's called the adjoint method.
segments.say: The trick is to run light backward. It's called the adjoint method.

segments.text: First, turn design into numbers: each pixel of the box gets a value p, from 0 for glass to 1 for silicon.
segments.say: First, turn design into numbers. Each pixel of the box gets a value, pee, from zero for glass, to one for silicon.

segments.text: A merit, F(p), scores the device: the fraction of light that reaches the two outputs.
segments.say: A merit, eff of pee, scores the device: the fraction of light that reaches the two outputs.

segments.text: Picture F as a landscape over all possible designs. To improve, walk uphill, along the gradient.
segments.say: Picture eff as a landscape, over all possible designs. To improve, walk uphill, along the gradient.

segments.text: The obvious way to find it: nudge one pixel, rerun the whole simulation, and see how F changes.
segments.say: The obvious way to find it: nudge one pixel, rerun the whole simulation, and see how eff changes.

segments.text: That's one simulation per pixel: four thousand for this little box, and millions for a metalens.
segments.say: That's one simulation per pixel: four thousand for this little box, and millions for a metalens.

segments.text: With a million pixels and a minute per simulation, one step uphill would take two years.
segments.say: With a million pixels, and a minute per simulation, one step uphill would take two years.

segments.text: Here's the way out. At one frequency, a wave simulation on a grid is one big linear system: A x = b.
segments.say: Here's the way out. At one frequency, a wave simulation on a grid is one big linear system: Eigh times ex, equals bee.

segments.text: b is the source, x is the field everywhere, and the matrix A holds the material, so it depends on p.
segments.say: Bee is the source, ex is the field everywhere, and the matrix, Eigh, holds the material, so it depends on pee.

segments.text: Differentiate both sides with respect to one pixel, and solve for how the field changes.
segments.say: Differentiate both sides with respect to one pixel, and solve for how the field changes.

segments.text: The merit's slope becomes a chain of three factors: a row, the inverse of A, and one column per pixel.
segments.say: The merit's slope becomes a chain of three factors: a row, the inverse of Eigh, and one column per pixel.

segments.text: Multiply right to left, and every column costs a solve with A: one simulation per pixel, again.
segments.say: Multiply right to left, and every column costs a solve with Eigh: one simulation per pixel, again.

segments.text: But multiply left to right! The row times A⁻¹ is a single vector, λ, and it takes just one extra solve.
segments.say: But multiply left to right! The row, times Eigh inverse, is a single vector, lambda, and it takes just one extra solve.

segments.text: Then each pixel's slope is a cheap product: two simulations give the whole gradient, however many pixels there are.
segments.say: Then each pixel's slope is a cheap product. Two simulations give the whole gradient, however many pixels there are.

segments.text: So what is λ, physically? Light obeys reciprocity: swap a source and a detector, and the signal stays the same.
segments.say: So what is lambda, physically? Light obeys reciprocity: swap a source and a detector, and the signal stays the same.

segments.text: In matrix terms, Aᵀ = A. So λ comes from the same simulation, with the source moved to the outputs: light sent backward.
segments.say: In matrix terms, Eigh transpose equals Eigh. So lambda comes from the same simulation, with the source moved to the outputs: light, sent backward.

segments.text: Nudge one pixel, and it scatters a tiny wavelet, with a strength set by the forward light hitting it.
segments.say: Nudge one pixel, and it scatters a tiny wavelet, with a strength set by the forward light hitting it.

segments.text: The backward field there tells how that wavelet reaches the outputs, and whether it arrives in step with the light already there.
segments.say: The backward field there tells how that wavelet reaches the outputs, and whether it arrives in step with the light already there.

segments.text: So each pixel's slope is the forward field times the adjoint field: the sensitivity map, for every pixel at once.
segments.say: So each pixel's slope is the forward field, times the adjoint field: the sensitivity map, for every pixel at once.

segments.text: Update every pixel, simulate again, and repeat. Watch the device take shape.
segments.say: Update every pixel, simulate again, and repeat. Watch the device take shape.

segments.text: Light run backward tells every pixel what to do.
segments.say: Light, run backward, tells every pixel what to do.

segments.text: You don't even need to derive adjoints by hand. Take a phase mask, then episode one's free-space propagation.
segments.say: You don't even need to derive adjoints by hand. Take a phase mask, then episode one's free space propagation.

segments.text: It's a chain: multiply by the mask, FFT, multiply by the transfer function H, inverse FFT, then square.
segments.say: It's a chain: multiply by the mask, F F T, multiply by the transfer function, aitch, inverse F F T, then square.

segments.text: Automatic differentiation, the engine of deep learning, runs the chain backward: FFTs become inverse FFTs, and H becomes its conjugate.
segments.say: Automatic differentiation, the engine of deep learning, runs the chain backward. F F Ts become inverse F F Ts, and aitch becomes its conjugate.

segments.text: For propagating waves, conjugating H just flips the sign of z. The backward pass really does send light backward.
segments.say: For propagating waves, conjugating aitch just flips the sign of zee. The backward pass really does send light backward.

segments.text: Now gradient descent shapes the mask to project any picture. Watch the image sharpen as the error falls.
segments.say: Now gradient descent shapes the mask to project any picture. Watch the image sharpen, as the error falls.

segments.text: Episode five's Gerchberg–Saxton loop was a clever heuristic; gradients make it an optimization with any goal.
segments.say: Episode five's Gurkberg Saxton loop was a clever heuristic. Gradients make it an optimization, with any goal.

segments.text: Now go further: design the optics and the software together.
segments.say: Now go further, and design the optics and the software together.

segments.text: A camera records a scene through our optics, adding noise; then an algorithm, here episode three's Wiener filter, sharpens it.
segments.say: A camera records a scene through our optics, adding noise. Then an algorithm, here episode three's Wiener filter, sharpens it.

segments.text: Compare the result with the truth, and send the gradient back through everything: the filter, the noise, the light, into the optics.
segments.say: Compare the result with the truth, and send the gradient back through everything: the filter, the noise, the light, into the optics.

segments.text: Ask for sharp images at every depth. An ordinary lens is sharp only in focus; elsewhere, its point-spread function, the PSF, blurs.
segments.say: Ask for sharp images at every depth. An ordinary lens is sharp only in focus. Elsewhere, its point spread function, the P S F, blurs.

segments.text: The learned optics gives up a perfect focus for a PSF that hardly changes with depth, which the filter can undo everywhere.
segments.say: The learned optics gives up a perfect focus, for a P S F that hardly changes with depth, which the filter can undo everywhere.

segments.text: In code, it's a three-line loop: simulate, take the gradient, step, a few hundred times.
segments.say: In code, it's a three line loop: simulate, take the gradient, step. A few hundred times.

segments.text: Real devices add rules: each pixel must be all silicon or all glass, with no feature too small to fabricate.
segments.say: Real devices add rules. Each pixel must be all silicon or all glass, with no feature too small to fabricate.

segments.text: The landscape has many hills, so different starting guesses climb to different designs: all good, none guaranteed best.
segments.say: The landscape has many hills, so different starting guesses climb to different designs: all good, none guaranteed best.

segments.text: And the optimizer exploits every error in its model: this lens shines in a cheap simulation, but loses half its light in a careful one.
segments.say: And the optimizer exploits every error in its model. This lens shines in a cheap simulation, but loses half its light in a careful one.

segments.text: So inverse design needs models fast enough to run thousands of times, and accurate enough to trust.
segments.say: So inverse design needs models fast enough to run thousands of times, and accurate enough to trust.

segments.text: One forward and one backward simulation give the gradient for every pixel at once.
segments.say: One forward and one backward simulation give the gradient for every pixel at once.

segments.text: And that completes our season: plane waves, lenses as Fourier transforms, the diffraction limit, coherence, phase, flat optics, periodic structures, trapped light, Maxwell on a grid, and design.
